summary: Gives recommendations to help implementers of IMAP4 clients and servers, since the protocol is rich and offers many choices and trade-offs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IMAP4 has many options, so clients and servers can make choices that do not work well together. RFC 2683 describes common trouble spots and ways to avoid them.

subtitle: Recommendations for IMAP4 client and server authors who want their implementations to interoperate.

tldr.problem: IMAP4 offers many implementation choices, and clients and servers can behave differently in ways that break interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: The memo gives practical recommendations for connections, scaling, valid requests, protocol details, and testing against other implementations.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2683 is an Informational memo and has been updated by RFC 7162.

sections.title: How to Read the Recommendations
sections.content:
RFC 2683 gives implementation advice for the IMAP4 protocol, which stores, retrieves, and manipulates electronic mail. It aims to help independent clients and servers work together despite the protocol's many options.

The memo uses lowercase words such as must, should, and may with meanings defined in the document. For example, must marks an action needed for interoperability, while may identifies an acceptable choice.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo is practical advice for people building IMAP mail programs. Its lowercase words such as “must” and “should” explain how strongly each recommendation matters.

sections.title: Handle Mailboxes and Connections Carefully
sections.content:
IMAP4 permits simultaneous access to one mailbox, but a server is not required to support it. A client must handle a second SELECT failing or causing another connection to close, and it should avoid opening the same mailbox more than once itself.

When ending a session, clients should send LOGOUT, wait for the tagged response, and close the socket. Servers should not expunge messages just because a connection closes; deletion requires an explicit command. If a server ends a connection, it should send a readable BYE response first. An inactivity timeout must not occur before at least 30 minutes of inactivity.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not assume a server allows the same mailbox to be opened twice. When a session ends, send a clear logout, and do not treat a closed connection as permission to delete mail.

sections.title: Limit Large Requests and Responses
sections.content:
Large mailbox lists, message lists, and message parts can overwhelm a client or keep a user waiting. The memo recommends listing one mailbox level at a time, fetching messages in batches, and downloading large body parts in pieces. Clients should normally fetch only the message parts they need.

Clients should keep command lines to about 1000 octets, excluding literals, and split very long requests. Servers should accept command lines of at least 8000 octets and return BAD when a command exceeds their limit. The memo also recommends that servers support UTF-8 searches and make flag searches fast.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask for large mailboxes and messages in smaller pieces. This limits the amount of data either side must handle at once.

sections.title: Use Capabilities and Follow Server Responses
sections.content:
Clients should use CAPABILITY to learn which IMAP version and extensions a server supports. They should not probe for features by sending commands, or send commands the server has not advertised as supported.

A server's responses also tell the client what operations a mailbox permits. For example, a client should not select a mailbox marked \Noselect or expunge a mailbox opened as read-only. Following these signals avoids requests the server already knows it cannot perform.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask the server which features it supports, then use only those features. Pay attention when the server says a mailbox cannot be selected or changed.

sections.title: Protocol Details That Commonly Cause Errors
sections.content:
The memo warns implementers to follow the protocol grammar exactly. Special characters in quoted strings need escaping, and carriage returns and line feeds may appear only in literals. Mailbox names use modified UTF-7 under the referenced protocol specification.

Servers should preserve UIDs when possible and change UIDVALIDITY when cached UIDs may no longer be valid. Clients must discard cached UID information when that value changes. FETCH responses may arrive in any order, in separate responses, or include unrequested updates, so clients must handle them whenever they arrive. The server's RFC822.SIZE value must be exact.

The memo's final recommendation is to test clients against many servers and servers against many clients.
sections.plainLanguage: Small formatting errors and stale message identifiers can cause real failures. Follow the exact syntax, handle replies in any order, and test with different mail programs.
